lesson.title: True, False, and Nothing Else: The bool Type
lesson.summary: The bool type holds exactly two values, True and False, produced by comparisons and logical operators, and it quietly doubles as a subtype of int inside Python.
lesson.body:
A boolean, written as bool in Python, can only ever hold one of two values: True or False. Booleans exist to represent the answer to a yes-or-no question inside a program, such as whether a number is even, whether a user has logged in, or whether a loop has finished. Every comparison you write, such as age >= 18 or name == "Maya", evaluates to a bool, and every if statement or while loop condition ultimately depends on getting a bool back so the program can decide which branch of code to run next.

Under the hood, bool is technically a subtype of int in Python: True behaves like the integer 1, and False behaves like the integer 0, wherever an integer is expected. This is why sum([True, True, False, True]) legally evaluates to 3, counting the True values as ones. This is a real and sometimes useful feature of the language, but it is worth treating bool as its own conceptual type in your own code, since writing True + True to mean 2 would be technically correct but confusing to anyone reading it later.

Booleans are produced automatically by comparison operators such as ==, !=, <, >, <=, and >=, and by the logical operators and, or, and not. Here is a short trace:

temperature = 95
is_hot = temperature > 90
is_safe = temperature < 100
print(is_hot and is_safe)

The comparison temperature > 90 evaluates to True, since 95 is greater than 90, so is_hot becomes True. The comparison temperature < 100 also evaluates to True, since 95 is less than 100, so is_safe becomes True. The expression is_hot and is_safe then evaluates to True as well, because and only produces True when both sides are True. The final print displays True.

Almost any value in Python can also be tested for truthiness even without an explicit comparison: the number 0, the empty string "", and the empty list [] are all treated as falsy in a boolean context, while nonzero numbers and non-empty containers are treated as truthy. This is why you will sometimes see if my_list: instead of if len(my_list) > 0:; both work, but only because Python is silently converting my_list to a bool behind the scenes. Understanding that conversion, rather than just memorizing the pattern, is exactly what the later lesson on implicit type conversion is about.

One more nuance worth knowing: and and or in Python do not always return a strict True or False; they return one of their actual operands, whichever one decided the outcome. print(0 or "default") displays "default", not True, because 0 is falsy so or moves on and returns its second operand exactly as given. print("hi" and "bye") displays "bye", not True, because "hi" is truthy so and evaluates the second operand and returns that instead. This behavior is called short-circuit evaluation, and it is why expressions like value = user_input or "N/A" are a common, compact way to supply a default value in real Python code.
